prompt: You plan the verification of a NEW finite element code before it is used for research. Its features: {"dimension": ["2D", "3D extruded section"], "geometry": ["straight edges", "inclined edges", "circular holes", "polygonal holes", "cylindrical hole through the thickness", "notch with a small root radius"], "material": ["linear elastic, isotropic", "compressible neo-Hookean"], "loading": ["constant traction (dead)", "pressure (linear)", "prescribed displacement"], "boundary": ["clamped", "symmetry / roller"], "analysis": ["static", "load stepping (finite strain)"], "outputs": ["point displacement", "strain energy", "region-averaged stress", "peak stress"]}. Elements: quadratic quadrilaterals and triangles in 2D, 27-node hexahedra and 10-node tetrahedra in 3D. Propose the set of verification benchmark problems (6 to 10) that would establish that the code is correct and how it converges, and for each: its purpose, the features it tests, the refinement studies to run, the convergence rates theory predicts (with the norm or quantity), the reference solution, and the literature that establishes it.

benchmarks.name: B1 - Constant-strain and quadratic-field patch tests (2D and 3D, linear elastic and neo-Hookean)
benchmarks.purpose: Show that every element type (quadratic quads and triangles, Hex27, Tet10) is consistent: it reproduces fields its interpolation contains exactly, to round-off, on distorted meshes. This is the minimum needed before any convergence study means anything.
benchmarks.features_tested: 2D and 3D extruded sections; straight and inclined edges (meshes with distorted, non-affine and skewed elements); linear isotropic material; compressible neo-Hookean with homogeneous finite deformation (uniaxial stretch, equibiaxial stretch, simple shear) driven by prescribed displacement and, separately, by dead traction; clamped and roller/symmetry BCs; load stepping; outputs: point displacement, strain energy, region-averaged stress.
benchmarks.refinement_studies: No refinement needed: run one coarse distorted patch per element type, plus a mesh-perturbation sweep (random interior node jitter up to about 30% of h) to show the result does not depend on distortion. For neo-Hookean, run 1, 5 and 20 load steps to the same final state and check the end state does not depend on the load path. Record Newton residual history per step.
benchmarks.expected_rates: No mesh rate. Displacements, stresses and energy should be exact to round-off (relative error around 1e-12 or better) for linear fields, and for linear elasticity also for complete quadratic displacement fields with the right body or traction data. Exception: 8-node serendipity quads on non-affine (non-parallelogram) shapes lose quadratic completeness, which is a known property of the element and not a bug. Q9, T6 (straight-sided), Hex27 and Tet10 should pass. Newton: quadratic convergence of the residual norm in the asymptotic iterations (e.g. 1e-3 -> 1e-6 -> 1e-12); linear convergence would mean an inconsistent tangent.
benchmarks.reference_solution: Closed form. Linear: an affine displacement field u = A x + b applied on the patch boundary, giving a uniform stress state. Finite strain: homogeneous deformation F = const, with Cauchy/PK1 stress computed in closed form from the compressible neo-Hookean strain energy the code implements (the exact W(F) form must be specified, e.g. the Ciarlet-Simo ln J or (J-1)^2 volumetric term). For dead-traction loading, apply the PK1 traction P·N that the closed form gives.
benchmarks.literature: Irons & Razzaque (1972); Taylor, Simo & Zienkiewicz (1986), 'The patch test - a condition for assessing FEM convergence', IJNME 22; Zienkiewicz, Taylor & Zhu, The Finite Element Method: Its Basis and Fundamentals, ch. on patch test; MacNeal & Harder (1985) standard test set (distorted-element shapes); Bonet & Wood, Nonlinear Continuum Mechanics for FEA (homogeneous deformation solutions, neo-Hookean forms); Wriggers, Nonlinear Finite Element Methods (Newton consistency).

benchmarks.name: B2 - Pure bending by linearly varying end traction (higher-order patch test, 2D and 3D extruded)
benchmarks.purpose: Check that linearly varying (non-constant) surface loads are integrated consistently, and that quadratic elements reproduce a quadratic displacement field exactly in a real boundary-value problem with statically determinate roller supports.
benchmarks.features_tested: 'Pressure (linear)' load: a linearly varying normal traction over the end face; symmetry/roller BCs; straight edges, plus a variant with the beam rotated so its edges are inclined to the global axes; 2D plane stress or plane strain, and the 3D extruded prism with roller faces; linear elastic; outputs: point displacement, strain energy, region-averaged stress, and peak stress (which is smooth here).
benchmarks.refinement_studies: Run 1x1, 2x2 and 4x4 element meshes with distorted variants to confirm the result is exact at every level, not merely converging. Also run a beam with a single row of elements and an aspect ratio sweep up to 1:20 to check for spurious locking or shear stiffening (none is expected for a quadratic field with these elements).
benchmarks.expected_rates: Exact to round-off at all mesh sizes for Q9, T6, Hex27 and Tet10 (displacement field quadratic, stress linear). Q8 is exact on parallelogram elements only. Load-vector check: the consistent nodal forces for a linear traction need an edge/face quadrature that is exact for degree 3 (linear load times quadratic shape function), so 2-point Gauss on edges is enough. Under-integration shows up as a mesh-dependent error.
benchmarks.reference_solution: Closed-form Saint-Venant pure-bending solution: sigma_xx = M y / I, all other stresses zero; quadratic displacement field (anticlastic curvature in plane stress/3D). Supports: roller at the neutral axis on the symmetry plane plus a single point pin to remove rigid modes, chosen so the exact solution satisfies them.
benchmarks.literature: Timoshenko & Goodier, Theory of Elasticity (3rd ed., 1970), pure bending of prismatic bars; MacNeal & Harder (1985), 'A proposed standard set of problems to test finite element accuracy', Finite Elem. Anal. Des. 1 (beam-type tests); Zienkiewicz & Taylor on consistent load vectors.

benchmarks.name: B3 - Thick-walled cylinder under internal pressure (Lamé), linear elastic, 2D quarter model and 3D extruded slice
benchmarks.purpose: Main smooth-solution convergence-rate benchmark with curved boundaries and pressure loading. It should show the optimal asymptotic rates for the quadratic elements and test isoparametric representation of circular boundaries.
benchmarks.features_tested: Circular holes and the cylindrical hole through the thickness; pressure load (follower in finite strain, but here linear and small strain); symmetry/roller BCs on the two cut planes; plane strain in 2D; in 3D, rollers on both end faces (plane strain) and a free-end variant; linear elastic; outputs: point displacement (bore radial displacement), strain energy, region-averaged hoop stress, peak hoop stress at the bore (smooth, so it must converge).
benchmarks.refinement_studies: Uniform h-refinement with at least 4 to 5 nested levels (e.g. 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 elements radially with proportional circumferential division), done separately for (a) isoparametric curved-edge elements and (b) straight-sided (subparametric) elements on the curved boundary. 3D: refine in-plane and through-thickness together; report against N_dof^{1/3}. Run with nu = 0.3 and with nu -> 0.49, 0.499 to expose volumetric locking.
benchmarks.expected_rates: Isoparametric quadratic elements, smooth solution: L2 displacement error O(h^3); H1-seminorm / energy-norm error O(h^2); strain-energy error |U - U_h| = O(h^4); nodal/point stress O(h^2) (possibly higher at superconvergent points); region-averaged stress at least O(h^2). In 3D, h ~ N_dof^{-1/3}. With straight-sided boundary elements, geometric error limits the energy-norm rate to about O(h^{3/2}) and the energy error to about O(h^3). Under pure pressure (traction) loading, U_h must approach U monotonically from below on nested meshes. Near-incompressibility: displacement-based quadratic elements lock moderately as nu -> 0.5, which shows up as a growing error constant (and pre-asymptotic rate loss) rather than divergence. Report this as a documented limitation, not a failure.
benchmarks.reference_solution: Closed-form Lamé solution: u_r = A r + B / r, with sigma_rr and sigma_thetatheta from the plane-strain (or generalized/open-end) form; strain energy per unit length in closed form; region averages by analytic integration.
benchmarks.literature: Lamé (1852); Timoshenko & Goodier, Theory of Elasticity, §§ on thick cylinders; Szabó & Babuška, Finite Element Analysis (1991) and Introduction to Finite Element Analysis (2011) for energy-norm rate theory; Ciarlet & Raviart (1972) / Lenoir (1986) on isoparametric curved boundaries and the geometric-error rate; Strang & Fix, An Analysis of the Finite Element Method (rates for degree-p elements).

benchmarks.name: B4 - Inflation of a thick cylinder made of compressible neo-Hookean material (finite strain Lamé)
benchmarks.purpose: Verify the finite-strain implementation (kinematics, constitutive law, consistent tangent, follower pressure, load stepping) against a reference solution that is independent of the FE code, and show that the optimal smooth-solution rates carry over to the nonlinear setting.
benchmarks.features_tested: Compressible neo-Hookean; load stepping to large strain (bore hoop stretch of at least 1.5); pressure load (follower in the deformed configuration) plus a variant with prescribed radial displacement at the bore (avoids the follower load); circular hole / cylindrical bore; symmetry/roller BCs; 2D plane strain and 3D extruded slice with end rollers; outputs: bore displacement, strain energy, region-averaged Cauchy hoop stress, peak hoop stress.
benchmarks.refinement_studies: (a) Mesh refinement at a fixed final load, with 4 to 5 nested levels as in B3. (b) Load-step refinement (e.g. 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 steps) at a fixed mesh to show that the converged static solution does not depend on step count, since a static hyperelastic problem is path-independent. Report the Newton iteration count and residual sequence per step. (c) A small-load limit: as p -> 0, the neo-Hookean solution must approach the B3 linear solution with relative difference O(p).
benchmarks.expected_rates: Same as B3 for the converged nonlinear solution: L2 displacement O(h^3), energy norm O(h^2), strain energy O(h^4), point stress about O(h^2), in 3D measured against N_dof^{-1/3}. Load-step study: no discretisation error in steps, so the final state should agree to within the Newton tolerance whatever the step count. Newton: quadratic convergence. For the follower pressure this needs the load-stiffness term in the tangent; omitting it gives linear convergence.
benchmarks.reference_solution: Semi-analytical: the axisymmetric radial deformation r = f(R) satisfies a nonlinear 2nd-order ODE (radial equilibrium) with traction or displacement BCs. Solve it with an independent high-accuracy BVP solver (e.g. collocation / shooting with tolerance about 1e-12) and report the solver tolerance. For the incompressible limit a closed-form solution exists and can be used as a cross-check of the nearly-incompressible trend. The exact W(F) used by the code must match the one used in the ODE.
benchmarks.literature: Rivlin (1949) and Ogden, Non-Linear Elastic Deformations (1984), ch. on cylindrical inflation; Holzapfel, Nonlinear Solid Mechanics (2000); Bonet & Wood (2008); Simo & Taylor (1991) / Simo & Hughes on consistent linearization and follower-load stiffness; Wriggers, Nonlinear Finite Element Methods (2008).

benchmarks.name: B5 - Plate with a central circular hole under remote uniaxial dead traction (Kirsch), 2D and 3D
benchmarks.purpose: Check stress concentration at a smooth hole: peak stress must converge here (there is no singularity), and both the region-averaged and peak stresses should converge at the smooth-solution rates.
benchmarks.features_tested: Circular hole; constant dead traction on the far edge; symmetry/roller BCs (quarter model); straight edges; linear elastic; 2D plane stress/strain and 3D extruded plate with a cylindrical through-hole; outputs: peak hoop stress at the hole edge, region-averaged stress in a small ring sector at the hole, point displacement at the hole, strain energy.
benchmarks.refinement_studies: Uniform h-refinement (4 to 5 levels) with isoparametric curved edges at the hole, at a fixed outer size. Separately run a domain-size study (W/D = 5, 10, 20, 40) to measure the truncation error, because only a constant-traction outer load is available (exact Kirsch tractions on a finite boundary are not). In 3D: through-thickness refinement plus a thickness/radius sweep, and refinement concentrated where the hole meets the free faces.
benchmarks.expected_rates: 2D, fixed domain: energy-norm O(h^2), strain energy O(h^4), peak (point) stress at the hole about O(h^2), region-averaged stress O(h^2) or better. 3D, where the bore meets the free surfaces: a weak vertex/edge singularity exists, so peak stress at that intersection may converge slowly or not at all. Peak stress at mid-thickness and region-averaged stress should still converge; energy rate may drop slightly below O(h^4) in N_dof^{-1/3} terms. The infinite-plate reference is approached as the truncation error (D/W)^2 shrinks; the mesh error must be separated from the domain error.
benchmarks.reference_solution: 2D: Kirsch closed-form infinite-plate solution (SCF of 3 for uniaxial tension in the infinite-plate limit). For a finite width use the published finite-width SCF curves/fits (Howland; Peterson's) or an overkill-mesh Richardson extrapolation from this code at a given W/D, stating which. 3D: through-thickness SCF variation from published 3D analyses; mid-plane values should approach the plane-strain result as thickness grows. There is no closed form at the bore/free-surface intersection.
benchmarks.literature: Kirsch (1898), VDI Zeitschrift 42; Timoshenko & Goodier, Theory of Elasticity; Howland (1930), Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 229; Pilkey & Pilkey, Peterson's Stress Concentration Factors (3rd ed., 2008); Folias & Wang (1990), Comput. Mech. 6 (3D hole in a plate); Kotousov & Wang (2002), Int. J. Eng. Sci. 40 (thickness effects).

benchmarks.name: B6 - Cook's membrane (tapered clamped panel with shear end load), linear elastic and compressible neo-Hookean
benchmarks.purpose: Test inclined edges and a clamped/free corner singularity on a standard, widely cross-coded problem. It shows that displacements and energy converge (at a reduced rate) while peak stress at the clamped corners does not converge.
benchmarks.features_tested: Inclined (non-parallel) edges producing skewed elements; clamped edge meeting traction-free edges (singular corners); constant dead shear traction on the free end; linear elastic and compressible neo-Hookean with load stepping; 2D plane strain/stress and 3D extruded with roller faces; outputs: tip vertical displacement, strain energy, region-averaged stress in an interior window, peak stress at the clamped corners.
benchmarks.refinement_studies: Uniform nested refinement (e.g. 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 elements per side), for both quadrilateral and triangular meshes. Optionally add a geometrically graded mesh toward the two clamped corners to show that the optimal rate comes back. For neo-Hookean: a fixed load with 10 to 20 steps and the same mesh sequence. 3D: extrude with rollers on the faces and compare with the 2D plane-strain result.
benchmarks.expected_rates: The solution is singular at the clamped-free corners with an exponent lambda (from the Williams eigen-equation for the corner angle, the clamped-free BCs and nu; lambda < 2, so it limits quadratic elements). Uniform meshes: energy-norm error O(h^{min(2, lambda)}) and strain-energy error O(h^{2 min(2, lambda)}); tip displacement converges at about the energy rate. Region-averaged stress away from the corners converges. Peak stress at the clamped corners is expected to keep growing with refinement (no convergence). This expected divergence is the test, and a 'converged' corner peak should be flagged as suspicious. Graded meshes restore O(N^{-1}) in energy norm per 2D DOF count (h^2 equivalent). Neo-Hookean: the same rate structure, with the singular exponent of the linearised corner problem governing the asymptotic behaviour.
benchmarks.reference_solution: Linear: published converged tip displacement from high-order or overkill computations (take the value and the exact problem data from the cited sources and do not paraphrase). Also a Richardson extrapolation from this code's sequence with the observed rate, which should be consistent with lambda. Neo-Hookean (compressible): no closed form, so use the code's own Richardson-extrapolated value cross-checked against an independent established FE code (e.g. FEniCS/deal.II/FEAP) using the same W(F) and parameters. Open question: which neo-Hookean form and parameter set to adopt, since literature values for Cook's membrane are given for differing formulations and are mostly nearly incompressible.
benchmarks.literature: Cook (1974), 'Improved two-dimensional finite element', J. Struct. Div. ASCE 100; Simo & Rifai (1990), IJNME 29 (linear reference values); Simo & Armero (1992), IJNME 33 (finite-strain Cook's membrane); Williams (1952), J. Appl. Mech. 19 (corner singularities); Szabó & Babuška (1991) on singular-solution rates and mesh grading.

benchmarks.name: B7 - L-shaped domain with a re-entrant corner (linear elastic)
benchmarks.purpose: Measure the reduced convergence rate caused by a known strong singularity with a precisely known exponent, and verify that graded/adaptive meshes recover optimal rates. It calibrates the pipeline's ability to tell 'non-convergent peak stress' from a bug.
benchmarks.features_tested: Polygonal re-entrant 270° corner (the polygonal-hole category); straight edges; constant dead traction or prescribed displacement; clamped and symmetry BCs; linear elastic; 2D and 3D extruded (rollers on faces; in 3D the re-entrant edge is a line singularity); outputs: strain energy, point displacement away from the corner, region-averaged stress away from the corner, peak stress at the corner.
benchmarks.refinement_studies: (a) Uniform nested h-refinement with 5 to 6 levels. (b) Geometric grading toward the corner (e.g. ratio 0.15 to 0.2, as in Szabó-Babuška). (c) Track region averages over a fixed sub-domain away from the corner and over a window that includes the corner, to show the averages converge where pointwise peaks do not.
benchmarks.expected_rates: For a 270° traction-free re-entrant corner the leading Williams exponents are lambda_I ≈ 0.5445 (symmetric) and lambda_II ≈ 0.9085 (antisymmetric), independent of nu for traction-free faces. Uniform meshes: energy-norm error O(h^{0.544}) and strain-energy error O(h^{1.089}), the same for quadratic as for linear elements (the singularity sets the rate, not p). Point displacement away from the corner and region averages converge, with the rate limited by the energy rate (up to about O(h^{1.09})). Peak stress at the corner diverges like h^{lambda_I - 1} ≈ h^{-0.456}. Graded meshes: optimal algebraic rate in N_dof is recovered. If clamped edges meet at the corner instead, the exponents differ and must be recomputed for nu.
benchmarks.reference_solution: Strain energy and stress-intensity coefficients from the Szabó-Babuška L-shape benchmark, which uses exact Williams-eigenfunction tractions. Open question: the code supports only constant traction, pressure and prescribed displacement, so it cannot apply the exact Williams tractions. Options: (i) add exact-traction loading for verification only; (ii) prescribe the exact displacement field on the outer boundary (piecewise interpolated, so it adds a boundary-data error that converges at the smooth rate); (iii) use a constant-traction variant with a Richardson reference whose extrapolation uses the known exponent 2*0.5445.
benchmarks.literature: Williams (1952), J. Appl. Mech. 19; Szabó & Babuška, Finite Element Analysis (Wiley 1991), L-shaped domain benchmark; Babuška & Miller / Babuška, Kellogg & Pitkäranta (1979) on graded meshes; Strang & Fix (1973) on singular rates.

benchmarks.name: B8 - Plate with a sharp-radius notch and an elliptical / polygonal hole (stress concentration resolution test)
benchmarks.purpose: Separate a large but finite stress concentration (small notch root radius rho or a sharp ellipse) from a true singularity (sharp-cornered polygonal hole). It shows that peak stress at a smooth notch converges only once h << rho, while at a sharp polygonal corner it never does.
benchmarks.features_tested: Notch with a small root radius; elliptical (curved) and polygonal (square/triangular) holes; constant dead traction; symmetry BCs; straight edges; linear elastic, with a neo-Hookean variant at moderate load; 2D and 3D extruded; outputs: peak stress at the notch root and corners, region-averaged stress in a fixed small window, strain energy, point displacement.
benchmarks.refinement_studies: Refinement parameterised by h/rho from about 2 down to about 0.02 near the notch root (local refinement with fixed far-field mesh, plus a uniform series). Repeat for rho/a = 0.1, 0.01, 0.001 to show how the pre-asymptotic window grows. For polygonal holes use uniform refinement and the window-average study.
benchmarks.expected_rates: Notch/ellipse: pre-asymptotic regime (h ≳ rho) where peak stress rises with refinement, looking like a singularity; asymptotic regime (h << rho) where peak stress converges at about O(h^2) and energy at O(h^4). The crossover should scale with rho, so peak-stress convergence must be judged against h/rho. Polygonal hole with sharp corners: the singular exponent comes from the Williams solution for the corner interior angle (traction-free faces). Energy error O(h^{2 lambda}) on uniform meshes; peak stress diverges as h^{lambda - 1}; region averages and far-field displacements converge.
benchmarks.reference_solution: Elliptical hole: Inglis closed form for the infinite plate, Kt = 1 + 2a/b, used with a domain-size study as in B5. Notch: published SCF charts/fits for the given geometry, or an overkill self-convergent solution with reported extrapolation uncertainty. Polygonal hole: no reference for the peak (it diverges by theory). Region averages and energy are referenced by Richardson extrapolation using the theoretical exponent.
benchmarks.literature: Inglis (1913), Trans. Inst. Naval Architects 55; Neuber, Kerbspannungslehre / Theory of Notch Stresses; Pilkey & Pilkey, Peterson's Stress Concentration Factors (2008); Williams (1952); Savin, Stress Concentration Around Holes (1961) for polygonal holes; Szabó & Babuška (1991).

benchmarks.name: B9 - 2D/3D consistency and 3D-specific checks (extruded sections with Hex27 and Tet10)
benchmarks.purpose: Show that the 3D implementation reproduces the 2D results whenever the 3D problem is posed as plane strain, and that 3D-only effects (through-thickness variation, free-surface corners) behave as theory predicts. It also checks the element families against each other.
benchmarks.features_tested: 3D extruded sections; 27-node hexahedra and 10-node tetrahedra; roller/symmetry faces enforcing plane strain; cylindrical hole through the thickness; clamped faces; dead traction, linear pressure and prescribed displacement; linear elastic and neo-Hookean with load stepping; all outputs.
benchmarks.refinement_studies: For B3, B5 and B6 geometries: (a) plane-strain extrusion (rollers on both faces) with one layer and with several layers, which must match the 2D solution on the same in-plane mesh; (b) free-face plate with in-plane plus through-thickness refinement, reported against N_dof^{1/3}; (c) the same problems with Hex27 versus Tet10 meshes of comparable N_dof.
benchmarks.expected_rates: (a) Plane-strain extrusion: with the same in-plane mesh and matching interpolation, 3D and 2D quadratic quad results (Hex27 vs Q9 extruded) should agree to solver tolerance; Tet10 vs T6 should agree to discretisation-error level and converge to the same limit. (b) Smooth regions: energy-norm O(h^2) = O(N_dof^{-2/3}), strain energy O(N_dof^{-4/3}), L2 O(N_dof^{-1}). Where clamped faces meet free faces, or the bore meets a free surface, edge/vertex singularities reduce the energy rate, and peak stress there is not expected to converge. Region averages and displacements away from those features still converge.
benchmarks.reference_solution: The verified 2D results from B3 to B6 (plane strain) as cross-references; closed forms (Lamé, Kirsch mid-plane plane-strain limit); for free-surface effects, published 3D through-thickness SCF variations plus self-convergent Richardson extrapolation.
benchmarks.literature: Folias & Wang (1990), Comput. Mech. 6; Kotousov & Wang (2002), Int. J. Eng. Sci. 40; Bažant & Estenssoro (1979), Int. J. Solids Struct. 15 (surface/vertex singularities); Szabó & Babuška (1991); Oberkampf & Roy, Verification and Validation in Scientific Computing (2010) for code-to-code and order-of-accuracy verification practice.
